forces.title: Medtech's value shift from hardware to software and AI
forces.description: The medtech industry is undergoing a structural shift where hardware categories are maturing and facing increasing price pressure. Software, particularly Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and AI-enabled solutions, is emerging as a critical avenue for differentiation, growth, and patient impact. This shift enables new recurring revenue models, embeds devices within broader clinical workflows, and unlocks new care models like remote monitoring and data-driven decision support, extending value beyond the point of care.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Medtech struggles with swift, compliant SaMD development
forces.description: Despite accelerating ambition in software development, the medtech industry struggles to deliver regulated Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) at the required pace. Traditional phased approaches, dictated by stringent regulatory and quality standards, extend timelines by 20-30% and significantly increase development costs, misaligning with agile software development methodologies. This inability to deliver high-quality SaMD without compromising regulatory-grade quality, while also integrating with hardware, presents a defining challenge for medtech organizations, hindering their capacity to capitalize on new growth avenues.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Cybersecurity threats for connected medical devices intensifying
forces.description: As connected devices, digital ecosystems, and AI-enabled capabilities expand within medtech, cybersecurity is becoming a critical dimension of software quality. Organizations must address these requirements throughout the development life cycle to meet evolving regulatory expectations and protect patient safety and trust. Recent advances in AI-driven vulnerability discovery are compressing the time between vulnerability identification and exploitation, escalating pressure on medtech organizations to continuously identify, remediate, and monitor software risks for their SaMD and integrated hardware products.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Medtech talent gap hinders digital innovation capability
forces.description: The medtech industry faces a significant structural challenge in attracting and retaining digital, technology, and analytics talent. Compared with adjacent industries, medtech is often perceived as less attractive, offering a lower employee value proposition and a limited availability of key technical skills, particularly in application development. This talent gap hinders the industry's ability to develop and deliver innovative Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) solutions at speed, impacting future growth and competitiveness in an increasingly software-driven market.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: AI integration streamlines SaMD development and quality assurance
forces.description: Leading medtech organizations are increasingly embedding AI across the software development life cycle for Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). This augments development teams by automating repeatable, compliance-heavy tasks and accelerating critical activities like documentation, testing, traceability, and risk analysis. These AI tools not only improve productivity and development efficiency but also enable a more consistent and scalable application of stringent quality and regulatory requirements, driving up to 50% reductions in low-value documentation effort and 10-15% increases in development capacity.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Early quality integration transforms SaMD development, reduces rework
forces.description: A fundamental shift is underway in medtech: embedding quality, regulatory, and risk management activities into the earliest stages of the software development life cycle for Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). This integrates quality into product definition, design, and development, moving away from traditional phase-based frameworks where quality checks are concentrated later. This approach reduces rework, improves auditability, and aligns agile development with regulatory expectations, leading to up to 50% reductions in low-value documentation and 10-15% increases in development capacity.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: UK's NHAP drives uptake of high-impact HealthTech
forces.description: The UK has launched the National HealthTech Access Programme (NHAP) as part of an ecosystem-wide approach to improve MedTech access. This program supports the uptake of high-impact technologies, including AI tools for prostate and breast cancer, and the capsule sponge for oesophageal cancer. By streamlining procurement and decision-making, NHAP aims to enable faster, more consistent adoption of proven innovations, better use of NHS resources, and long-term value for patients, ultimately accelerating the integration of advanced medical devices and equipment into healthcare.
forces.source_title: Life Sciences Sector Plan: One Year On

forces.title: NHS shifts to value-based procurement for MedTech
forces.description: New national guidance for Value Based Procurement has been introduced in the UK, signaling a strategic shift for the NHS in how it acquires medical technology. This initiative aims to prioritize patient outcomes, long-term value, and sustainability over just upfront cost when purchasing medical devices and equipment. This structural change is designed to facilitate earlier access to proven innovations, enable more consistent and efficient procurement decisions, and ensure better use of NHS resources, creating a more sustainable innovation pathway for the MedTech sector.
forces.source_title: Life Sciences Sector Plan: One Year On

forces.title: MHRA streamlines medical device regulation, advances new model
forces.description: The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in the UK has reduced regulatory barriers and is advancing towards a new device regulatory model. This includes securing funding for a third phase of AI Airlock, indicating a focus on AI-enabled medical technologies. These efforts aim to simplify processes and improve market access for innovative medical devices and equipment, ensuring that new technologies can reach patients faster while maintaining safety and efficacy standards, fostering a more agile and responsive regulatory environment.
forces.source_title: Life Sciences Sector Plan: One Year On

forces.title: Improved health data access fuels MedTech innovation
forces.description: The UK is strengthening its R&D foundations by establishing the Health Data Research Service and advancing policy reforms to enable secure, efficient access to health data for research and innovation. Major programs such as Our Future Health and the NHS Genomic Medicine Service are scaling up, creating world-leading research assets. This improved access to health data is a significant tailwind for the Medical Devices & Equipment sector, as it powers the development of AI-enabled diagnostic hardware, personalized medical technologies, and data-driven solutions, accelerating innovation from early-stage research to clinical application.
forces.source_title: Life Sciences Sector Plan: One Year On

forces.title: Global medtech market growth creates export opportunities
forces.description: The global medical device market (excluding IVD) is valued at USD $583 billion and is forecast to grow at a CAGR of 5.5% through 2030, with Asia-Pacific leading this expansion at 6.9% CAGR. This growth is driven by aging populations, expanding chronic disease burdens, and a severe shortage of healthcare workers globally, increasing demand for solutions that enhance efficiency and access. This robust international demand presents significant export opportunities for UK medical device and equipment manufacturers, particularly for innovative and value-based products.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: Globalization intensifies MedTech R&D and innovation
forces.description: The medtech market is experiencing a significant structural shift driven by globalization, with the Asia-Pacific region's share of global medtech research increasing from 29% in 2012 to 36% in 2022, and over two-thirds of global patent filings in 2023 originating there. This intensifies global competition but also fosters collaboration and opens up new markets for UK firms. UK companies must adapt to this evolving landscape, focusing on strong clinical and economic evidence, robust IP strategies, and global commercialization to compete and benefit from increased innovation worldwide.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: Digital-first medtech and AI diagnostics see rapid global growth
forces.description: The global market is experiencing rapid growth in digital-first medtech and AI-driven diagnostics, exemplified by South Korea's software-only medtech exports growing at a 312% average annual rate from 2019-2023. The country's Digital Medical Products Act further establishes regulatory pathways for AI diagnostics and SaMD. This trend signals a global embrace of software as a core value driver in medical devices, presenting a significant upside opportunity for UK firms specializing in AI-enabled diagnostic hardware and SaMD, but also intensifying global competition in this innovative segment.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: Global scarcity of regulatory and clinical talent for medtech
forces.description: Across the global medtech landscape, there is a scarcity of professionals with deep experience in navigating complex regulatory submissions (like FDA De Novo and PMA), managing trials to ISO 14155 standards, and building ISO 13485-compliant quality systems. This talent gap, particularly pronounced in the Asia-Pacific region, can lead to significant delays and setbacks for companies trying to launch innovative 'me-first' devices internationally. For UK firms, this implies intensified competition for skilled personnel and highlights the need to cultivate robust in-house expertise or strategically engage specialist consultants for successful global expansion.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: Inadequate IP protection for novel medtech innovations
forces.description: Many emerging medtech companies, particularly in the Asia-Pacific region, initiate their intellectual property (IP) strategies too late, significantly limiting their strategic options. While delaying global IP filings might work for 'me-better' devices competing on cost, it is highly risky for genuinely novel products. Gaps in patent coverage in key global markets like the US, EU, or Japan can compress valuations or narrow exit opportunities during critical negotiations for licensing, partnership, or acquisition. For UK medtech firms, this highlights a crucial risk and underscores the imperative for proactive, comprehensive global IP strategies from the earliest development stages to safeguard innovations.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: New medtech faces significant reimbursement and evidence hurdles
forces.description: For novel medical devices, achieving regulatory approval is just the initial step; significant challenges remain in securing reimbursement and generating sufficient clinical and economic evidence. In the US, less than half of FDA-authorized devices achieve Medicare coverage, with a median wait of nearly six years. In the EU and Japan, evolving Health Technology Assessment (HTA) frameworks demand increasingly higher evidence, including comparative effectiveness data. This global challenge requires UK medtech firms to integrate reimbursement and evidence strategies early in their clinical programs, as success hinges on demonstrating value beyond regulatory clearance.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: Increased competition and changing M&A landscape from Asia-Pacific MedTech
forces.description: Western multinational corporations (MNCs) in medtech, including those in the UK, face a changing competitive landscape as Asia-Pacific-originated medtechs move from import substitutes to globally recognized innovators. To succeed, Western MNCs must transition from 'selling in' to 'buying from' or co-creating with Asia-Pacific firms. This shift indicates intensified competition for market share and innovation, as well as evolving M&A and partnership dynamics. UK firms must adapt by proactively identifying early-stage innovations, establishing learn-and-transfer loops, and making Asia-Pacific-first innovation repeatable to capture global growth.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: Reimbursement readiness guides medtech market entry strategy
forces.description: Successful medtech market entry increasingly relies on strategically sequencing markets based on reimbursement and standard-of-care readiness, rather than solely regulatory clearance. The Biobot Surgical case exemplifies this, where entry into the US market was delayed until dedicated CPT codes for transperineal prostate biopsies were issued in 2026, despite earlier regulatory approval in other regions. This approach minimizes commercial risk and maximizes return on investment, underscoring that UK medtech firms must treat reimbursement and standard-of-care readiness as critical inputs for market strategy, not post-approval challenges.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: UK government policies enhance MedTech ecosystem and export support
forces.description: Governments and ecosystem builders, including those in the UK, are increasingly focused on strengthening the MedTech ecosystem to help promising innovations reach global markets. Key priorities include funding talent development, establishing translation hubs, industrializing evidence generation with international standard-compliant clinical infrastructure, driving regulatory alignment with global standards, and providing global export support. These policy interventions aim to remove structural barriers, enhance the UK's competitiveness, and ensure that medical devices and equipment can scale internationally, improving market access and commercial viability for UK firms.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: UK's rising AI productivity to benefit MedTech innovation
forces.description: AI is projected to significantly boost UK labor productivity by 3.4% over the next decade, contributing to a 1.7% increase in AI-driven GDP. This broader national adoption and impact of AI create a positive economic backdrop for the Medical Devices & Equipment sector. Specifically, it fosters an environment conducive to the development and integration of AI-enabled diagnostic hardware and advanced medical devices, leveraging national expertise and investment in AI to drive innovation and efficiency within the sector.
forces.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

viewpoints.title: Software is reshaping medtech value, offering new differentiation and growth avenues
viewpoints.description: McKinsey views software as a critical avenue for differentiation, growth, and patient impact in the medtech industry, as hardware categories mature and face increasing price pressure. This structural shift is enabling new recurring revenue models, embedding devices within broader clinical workflows, and unlocking novel care models like remote monitoring and data-driven decision support. Advances in AI are further improving software productivity by 30-70%, making the integration of regulated software (SaMD) into digital ecosystems an imperative for value creation.
viewpoints.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

viewpoints.title: UK Government initiatives boosting HealthTech access and value-based procurement
viewpoints.description: The UK Government is actively improving access and procurement for HealthTech through initiatives like the National HealthTech Access Programme (NHAP), designed to enable faster, fairer access to innovative technologies across England and Wales. Furthermore, new Value Based Procurement standard guidance has been published to help the NHS assess wider value, not just purchase price, when buying medical technology. These efforts are part of a broader Life Sciences Sector Plan aiming to position the UK as a leading life sciences economy by 2030.
viewpoints.source_title: Life Sciences Sector Plan: One Year On

demand_drivers.description: Increased prevalence of age-related conditions requiring medical devices and equipment, driving market demand globally.
Rising rates of chronic diseases necessitating ongoing diagnostics, monitoring, and treatment via medical devices, globally.
Drives demand for medical devices and equipment that enable providers to increase efficiency and do 'more with less,' such as automation, AI-enabled diagnostics, and remote monitoring systems.

demand_drivers.driver: Government initiatives to accelerate patient access
demand_drivers.description: Policy actions, such as streamlined regulatory pathways and value-based procurement, are designed to shorten the time it takes for innovative medical technologies to reach patients, thereby increasing their adoption and market footprint.

new_opportunities.description: The UK aims to improve its ranking for patient access to medical technologies, moving from mid-range in Europe to top three. This accelerated and more consistent access presents significant opportunities for medical device manufacturers to see faster adoption and commercial success for their innovations.
new_opportunities.opportunity: Faster and more consistent patient access to innovative medical technologies

market_sizing.methodology: The UK government's Life Sciences Sector Plan aims for the UK to be among the top three fastest in Europe for patient access to medical technologies by 2030, indicating a focus on accelerating market adoption and value realization.
market_sizing.source_title: Life Sciences Sector Plan: One Year On
